draft.title: Strengths and limits of budgetary policy
card: Strength
Budgetary policy can be aimed at particular regions or groups. For example, spending can go to a drought-hit area or to low-income households.
Limit: time
A change must be planned, usually announced in the budget and passed by Parliament. By then the economic problem may have changed, so the effect can come late.
Limit: debt
When the government spends more than it collects, it borrows. That debt must be repaid later, with interest, which can limit future spending.
So the budget can be precise about who it helps, but it is often slow and can leave a cost for later.
draft.remember: Budgetary policy can be targeted, but it can be slow and leaves debt to repay.

a.q: Which is a strength of budgetary policy compared with a policy that affects the whole economy?
opts: It can be aimed at a particular region or group
It takes effect as soon as it is announced
It never needs to be repaid because it is spending
It does not need Parliament to approve changes
a.why: Spending and tax measures can be aimed at a chosen region or group, such as a flood-hit town. The other options are wrong because budget changes take time to plan and pass, and borrowing must be repaid.
a.clue: Think about who can receive the help.

b.q: A government approves extra spending on jobs programs after a downturn. By the time the programs start, the economy has already recovered. Which limit does this show?
opts: The time it takes to plan and pass changes
The need to repay debt with interest
The difficulty of aiming spending at a group
The loss of tax revenue from lower incomes
b.why: The delay between the problem and the programs starting is the time limit. Debt repayment is a different limit, because this case is about timing and not about borrowing. The scenario says nothing about targeting.
b.clue: Focus on when the help arrived, not how it was paid for.

a.best: It can be aimed at a particular region or group

b.best: The time it takes to plan and pass changes
